title: Low blood sugar: the brain notices
description: Low blood sugar, or hypoglycaemia, is most common in people treating diabetes with insulin. When blood sugar falls, the body sounds an alarm: a faster heart, sweating, shakiness, hunger. The episode follows what the brain does as blood sugar falls in healthy volunteers, and describes how this response can fade in some people with type 1 diabetes, which makes low blood sugar harder to notice.
caveat: The blood-flow finding comes from one study of nine healthy volunteers whose blood sugar was lowered under careful medical control; another study of healthy volunteers found changes in more areas but, in the abstract read, without saying in which direction. Blood flow is used as a stand-in for activity. Overall blood flow to the brain fell slightly during low blood sugar while the areas drawn became relatively more active. These are mild, controlled episodes in a research setting.

phases.name: Blood sugar falls
phases.caption: Blood sugar drops below its usual level, here under careful control in a research setting.

phases.name: The body's alarm
phases.caption: The body responds: heart rate and stress hormones rise. In the brain, the anterior cingulate and the thalamus on both sides become more active, while overall blood flow to the brain falls slightly.

order.rationale: Blood flow was measured during steady low and normal blood sugar, not as it fell. Placing the alarm after the fall is how the procedure was done.

phases.name: When the alarm fades
phases.caption: In some people with type 1 diabetes who no longer notice low blood sugar, the brain shows no response at all, and the body's warning signs are weaker. This is described, not drawn: the brain stays as in the healthy response above.

order.rationale: This comes from a separate group of people with diabetes, compared at one time point.

phases.name: Blood sugar restored
phases.caption: Blood sugar returns to normal and the brain settles. The return was not measured in the sources read; this last part is an assumption.

order.rationale: No source read measured the brain as blood sugar recovered. The return to rest is assumed.

regions.explanation: More active during low blood sugar, on both sides, in one study of nine healthy volunteers. The study calls this area the medial prefrontal cortex and identifies it as Brodmann areas 24 and 32, which make up the anterior cingulate, drawn here. Blood flow is used as a stand-in for activity.
